profile.summary: 2 Chronicles present the history of Judah as a word of encouragement to a people without political independence and with seemingly uncertain future. The book recalls the past from the reign of Solomon to the fall of Jerusalem, but it does so with a pastoral and theological purpose: to show that God's promises to David and the temple remain firm, even after exile. The narrative highlights the centrality of the right cult, prayer, repentance and God's response to faithfulness or the infidelity of his people. Although the kingdom of Judah ended in ruin, the book ends with an opening for restoration, pointing to the hope of the return promoted by Cyrus.
profile.setting: The historical setting goes from the united monarchy and divided into Babylonian exile and the beginning of the return. The fall of Judah occurred between 605 and 586 BC; the book was probably composed of around 400 BC in Persian period, although the exact date and authorship are discussed. The author, called the Cronist, writes to the Jewish community already back to Jerusalem, now without Davidic king and under foreign rule. His interest is not to replace other historical narratives, but to reinterpret the past in the light of the spiritual and identity needs of his time, with special attention to the temple, the priesthood and the promises made by God.

structure.label: Solomon and the construction of the temple
structure.description: The narrative focuses on Solomon's reign, especially in the building of the temple, in the organization of worship and in the prayer of dedication, with the divine response emphasizing judgment, repentance and restoration.

structure.label: The Divided Kingdom and the Centrality of Judah
structure.description: After the division, the focus lies almost entirely on Judah and its kings, showing the link between Davidic continuity, Jerusalem and the temple, without ignoring contacts with the north.

structure.label: Kings of Judah and paths of faithfulness and fall
structure.description: The book features several reigns of Judah, contrasting reforms, prosperity, and infidelity, and emphasizing that obedience brings blessing while disobedience brings discipline.

structure.label: The reforms of Hezekiah
structure.description: Hezekiah emerges as a great reformer, with restoration of temple worship, religious organization and careful preparation in the face of the Assyrian threat.

structure.label: Manasseh, Ammon and Josiah
structure.description: These chapters show the corruption that contributes to the ruin of Judah, but also the surprising humiliation and restoration of Manasseh, and then the godly reign of Josiah.

structure.label: Fall of Jerusalem and hope of return
structure.description: The book concludes with the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, exile in Babylon, and finally the proclamation of Cyrus, which paves the way for return and reconstruction.

themes: God's faithfulness to the promises made to David
The centrality of the temple and the correct worship
The value of prayer, repentance and humility
The relationship between obedience, judgment, and restoration
Hope for Restoration for God's People
readingKeys: Notice how the author selects and organizes the episodes to highlight the temple, Jerusalem and the dynasty of David.
Realize the repeated pattern of sin, prophetic warning, judgment, and possibility of repentance.
Compare the reigns presented as examples of reformation or ruin, especially Hezekiah, Manasseh and Josiah.
profile.cautions: 2 Chronicles is not intended to be a neutral repetition of all history, but a pastoral and theological re-reading of the past. The book emphasizes certain kings, omits or reduces other details and interprets the events from the post-exile people's situation. Thus, it should be read with attention to his purpose: to strengthen hope, to call to fidelity and to remember that God rules history and fulfills his promises.

dossier.narratedEra: From the time of Solomon and the construction of the temple until the fall of Jerusalem, Babylonian exile and the decree of Cyrus (Steen centuries BC), with occasional retreats to Israel's previous history in the introductory notes.
dossier.compositionEra: Written around 400 BC, after exile, when Judah already lived as a small province of the Persian Empire. The notes call the author only "Chronicler" and do not name a specific traditional author; the main point is that the book speaks to post-exile readers, under Persian domination, from its own historical and theological perspective.

politics.title: Judah without Davidic King under Persian rule
politics.detail: The introduction describes the restored community as a descended kingless people of David, living as Persian subjects and without immediate prospect of being an independent kingdom.
politics.readingImpact: This shifts reading to post-exile: 2 Chronicles is not only memory of the past, but a response to a politically small community without sovereignty, encouraging hope in divine promises.

politics.title: Davidic dynasty and temple as axis of continuity
politics.detail: The notes claim that the Cronist associates the continuity of the kingdom and the future of Israel with the David dynasty and the temple in Jerusalem; the history of Judah is narrated in the light of this bond.
politics.readingImpact: Political legitimacy is read in terms of covenant and worship: the real power is not neutral, but assessed by the relationship with the temple and with the promises to David.

politics.title: Division of the kingdom and relationship between north and south
politics.detail: The summary says that the Cronista does not treat the division only as the northern fault: he sees the northern kingdom as part of Israel that needed to be restored and gives special attention to contacts between north and south. He also notes that the north sometimes did what was right.
politics.readingImpact: Reading Israel's internal tensions gains nuance: the division does not automatically end hope, and episodes of cooperation or return become theologically relevant.

politics.title: Alliance of Jehoshaphat with Ahab and the entrance of Athaliah in Judah
politics.detail: The notes of 2 Chronicles 18 say that Jehoshaphat's covenant with Ahab compromised his faithfulness to the Lord, and that the marriage of the son of Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, with Ataliah brought the apostasy of Israel to Judah.
politics.readingImpact: The political context appears as spiritual risk: dynastic alliances are not only diplomacy, but paths by which Israel's infidelity invades Judah.

politics.title: Egyptian intervention in the succession of 609 BC.
politics.detail: In 2 Cr 36, Pharaoh Neco interferes immediately after the enthronement of Jeoacaz, installs Eliaquim in his place and gives him the name Jehoiakim.
politics.readingImpact: Succession in Judah is not presented as autonomous: internal policy is subordinate to international pressures, which reinforces the reading of national vulnerability before the fall.

politics.title: Babylon, destruction and permission to return
politics.detail: The summary traces the series of Babylonian attacks that culminates in the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple, followed by the proclamation of Cyrus that allows the return and reconstruction.
politics.readingImpact: The political end of Judah is not the end of history; the conquest-forward sequence structures the hope of the book.

customs.title: Public trip from Solomon to Gibeon for sacrificial worship
customs.detail: 2 Chronicles 1:2-6 is described as a major public endeavor linked to Solomon's access to the throne, with military commanders and clan leaders. The text associates the place with the tabernacle and the great bronze altar, where sacrifices were offered regularly.
customs.readingImpact: The episode shows that the legitimization of the reign passes through public worship; political authority and worship appear together at the beginning of Solomon's reign.

customs.title: Priested and Provision for the Temple
customs.detail: The introduction highlights that much of the first nine chapters deals with the construction of the temple and the provision for priests. The focus of the book is less on dynastic curiosity and more on how the cult is organized and sustained.
customs.readingImpact: This guides the reading of 2 Chronicles as a history of worship: the temple is not a secondary setting, but the center of community life.

customs.title: Prayer, Repentance and Divine Response in the Worship
customs.detail: The notes on 2 Chronicles 6:1-7:22 say that Solomon's prayer and God's answer articulate the prospect of the Cronist: God answers the prayers and repentance of his people, judging disobedience, but rewarding humility, prayer, healing and deliverance.
customs.readingImpact: The cultual practice is not mechanical; the reader is led to understand prayer and repentance as real means of relationship with God in the post-exile community.

customs.title: Easter of Hezekiah as a model of restoration
customs.detail: The notes claim that Hezekiah invited the north to participate in the first Passover of his reign, which many answered, and that a similar celebration had not occurred since the days of Solomon.
customs.readingImpact: Easter becomes a sign of restored unity; the cultual rite is read as a concrete proposal for Israel's reunification.

customs.title: Oath of allegiance in the name of God
customs.detail: In 2 Cr 36:13, the oath imposed on Zedekiah is explained as an oath of vassalage probably similar to the Assyrian treatises, made in the name of the vassal god.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the breaking of the oath is not only a political act, but solemn infidelity before God, which deepens the gravity of rebellion.

customs.title: The sabbath rest of the earth after exile
customs.detail: The note of 2 Chronicles 36:21 says that the land finally enjoyed its sabbatical rest, relating exile to punishment for disobedience and the time of restoration.
customs.readingImpact: Exile is interpreted in ritual and theological categories: even the earth enters the drama of the covenant, which extends the reading of the catastrophe.

language.title: Selective rewrite from previous sources
language.detail: The introduction states that the Cronista carefully selected his material and re-emplore it for his own purposes, without intending to replace or supplement the previous historical writings.
language.readingImpact: The reader should observe that 2 Chronicles is a theologically shaped narrative; omissions and expansions are part of the literary method of the book.

language.title: "Shapat" as "government" in addition to "judge"
language.detail: In 2 Chronicles 1:10, the note says that the Hebrew shapat, often translated as "judge," can also mean "government."
language.readingImpact: Solomon's wisdom is presented not only as legal discernment, but as a capacity to exercise legitimate government.

language.title: Josafá's speech as a synthesis of the book
language.detail: The introduction takes the words of Jehoshaphat in 2 Chronicles 20:20 as a capture of the spirit of the book: to trust in the Lord and in his prophets to stand firm and prosper.
language.readingImpact: This shows that the programmatic language of 2 Chronicles is exhortation; the book reads the story to form obedient confidence, not just to record facts.

language.title: Tom of Micaiah and contrast with the prophets of the court
language.detail: The note of 2 Chronicles 18:15 notes that Micaiah's response may have sounded ironic or used the same words as his rivals; the 400 voices of the cut are described as "yes-men" of Ahab.
language.readingImpact: The episode gains rhetorical strength: authentic prophetic language is put in contrast to power-accommodated language.

language.title: Omissions and expansions as a narrative resource
language.detail: The introduction says that the Cronist extends the portrait of kings such as Uzziah, Jotham and Hezekiah, while omitting certain episodes of Kings, such as the attempted coup of Adonijah and Solomon's sins.
language.readingImpact: These choices shape the reading of the reign: the focus falls on fidelity, temple and reformation, rather than about real scandal.

language.title: The image of a "new exodus"
language.detail: The conclusion of 2 Chronicles is linked to Cyrus' permission and the expression of a new exodus, in continuity with Isaiah 40:1-11.
language.readingImpact: Post-exile restoration is narrated with liberation language; the return is not mere political movement, but redemptive resumption.

timeline.title: Fall of Judah and the timeline distance of the book
timeline.detail: The introduction places the Babylonian conquest of Judah between 605 and 586 BC, about two centuries before 2 Chronicles was written, around 400 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: This helps to read the book as a late reflection on a past already distant, aimed at answering post-exile questions.

timeline.title: Death of Josiah and the beginning of the end
timeline.detail: Josiah died in 609 BC, and the end of Judah came soon after. According to the introduction, in four years the Babylonians began the series of attacks that led to the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple.
timeline.readingImpact: The text presents the fall as a historical process in escalation, not as an isolated event, reinforcing the link between infidelity and national collapse.

timeline.title: Jehoacaz, Jehoiakim and the final chronology of Judah
timeline.detail: Jehoahaz reigned three months in 609 BC; Jehoiakim reigned from 609 to 598 BC; Jehoiachin was taken captive in 597 BC, and Zedekiah reigned from 597 to 586 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The short and unstable sequence of the last kings accelerates the feeling of inevitability of ruin, preparing the reader for exile.

timeline.title: Capture of Joaquim and long wait in exile
timeline.detail: The note identifies the capture of Joaquim on 16 March 597 BC, his trip to Babylon about a month later and his captive stay for thirty-seven years.
timeline.readingImpact: The king's personal exile predicts in miniature the collective exile of the nation and sustains the hope of further restoration.

timeline.title: Destruction of the temple and sense of judgment
timeline.detail: The temple was destroyed in August 586 BC, and the note links the length of captivity to Jeremiah's prophecy and the sabbatical rest of the earth.
timeline.readingImpact: The ruin of the temple is not a military accident; it is read as covenant judgment with defined theological and chronological significance.

timeline.title: Decree of Cyrus and opening of restoration
timeline.detail: In 538 BC, Cyrus of Persia allowed the community of Judah to return and rebuild Jerusalem; the introduction calls this the hopeful endpoint of the book.
timeline.readingImpact: The outcome prevents a total defeat reading: the story ends in promise, not in abandonment.

investigation: As the emphasis on temple, priesthood and prayer organizes the political memory of Judah throughout 2 Chronicles.
How the expansions on Hezekiah, Jehoshaphat and Solomon serve the post-exile purpose of hope and restoration.
As the reading of the north and south avoids a simplistic condemnation of the division and seeks to imagine reunification.
What relationship the Cronist establishes between infidelity, international crisis and divine judgment in the final chapters.
How the conclusion with Cyrus functions as a literary and theological bridge for Ezra, according to the notes provided.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends only on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry for 2 Chronicles; therefore it covers mainly the general introduction and some specific chapters (1, 18 and 36). Many sections of the book have not received a note here, so it is not appropriate to generalize custom, political or language for the whole corpus without textual support. Some statements are explicitly interpretative in the sources, especially the theological readings of post-exile, division of the kingdom and the editorial choices of the Cronist. There are also points debated in the notes themselves, such as the translation of 1:16 and the hue of 18:15; when this occurs, the item was marked as debated or interpretation, without turning into fact. No speculative chronologies were used other than the dates and tracks explicitly provided in the sources.
